title: Quantification of Vertical Ground Reaction Forces of Popular Bilateral Plyometric Exercises
authors: Wallace BJ, Kernozek TW, White JM, Kline DE, Wright GA, Peng H, Huang C
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 14 power-oriented collegiate and national-level track and field men; not runners and not recreational athletes
findings: Each man performed 3 trials of 9 bilateral plyometric exercises in one session: depth drops (DD) and depth jumps (DJ) from 30, 60 and 90 cm, a vertical jump (VJ), a standing long jump (SLJ) and 2 consecutive jumps (2CJ). Peak impact vertical ground reaction forces were normalised to body weight.

The 90 cm depth drop, the 90 cm depth jump, the 60 cm depth drop and the standing long jump peaked significantly higher than the vertical jump: 5.39, 4.93, 4.30 and 4.22 times body weight against 3.34 times body weight for the vertical jump.
The 30 cm depth jump peaked at 2.78 times body weight, insignificantly lower than the vertical jump, and the standing long jump peaked higher than the 2 consecutive jumps (p <= 0.05).
limitations: Fourteen collegiate and national-level power athletes in one session; peak impact force of landing only, not the rate of loading, the tissue load, the number of contacts or any injury outcome; none of the movements are the low-amplitude on-the-spot hops of a beginner ladder. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: Landing force rises steeply with drop height: depth drops from 60 and 90 cm and depth jumps from 90 cm peaked at about 4.3-5.4 times body weight against about 3.3 for a vertical jump. It supports leaving depth jumps and drops out of a plan for recreational runners, for which the corpus has no dose or bone-stress data, and it does not measure the engine's own movements.
No claim that a given movement is safe or unsafe follows from a peak force.
